title: Stacks & Queues
tagline: Two disciplined access patterns — LIFO and FIFO — that power everything from undo history to BFS.

sections.content:
Stacks and queues are not exotic data structures — they are **disciplined access policies** layered on top of arrays or linked lists. A stack enforces Last-In First-Out (LIFO): you can only add and remove from the same end. A queue enforces First-In First-Out (FIFO): you add to one end and remove from the other. This single constraint — limiting where you touch the collection — turns a generic sequence into a powerful abstraction.

These structures appear everywhere in real systems. The JavaScript call stack, browser history, undo/redo — all stacks. BFS graph traversal, event loops, OS process scheduling — all queues. Knowing when to reach for each, and understanding the O(1) operations that make them efficient, is a core interview and day-to-day engineering skill.

sections.title: A Plate Pile vs a Ticket Line
sections.content:
A **stack** is like a pile of plates in a cafeteria. You always add a plate to the top and always take from the top — the last plate placed is the first removed. This LIFO behaviour is exactly how the call stack works: each function call is pushed; when it returns it is popped, restoring the previous frame.

A **queue** is like a ticket line at a theme park. The first person in line is the first to board the ride — FIFO. This fairness property makes queues right for BFS traversal, task scheduling, and print spoolers: items are processed in the exact order they arrived, with no cutting allowed.

A **stack** exposes three operations: `push(item)` adds to the top, `pop()` removes and returns the top item, and `peek()` reads the top without removing it. All three are O(1). Stacks are trivially implemented with a JavaScript array using `push` and `pop` — both already O(1) amortised at the array end. The key discipline is never accessing the array from any other position.

A **queue** exposes `enqueue(item)` at the rear and `dequeue()` from the front. The classic mistake is implementing a queue with a JavaScript array and using `shift()` for dequeue — `shift` is O(n) because it shifts every element left. Correct O(1) queue implementations use a **linked list** (head = front, tail = rear) or a **circular buffer** (fixed-size array with head and tail indices that wrap around modulo capacity).

A **deque** (double-ended queue) supports O(1) insertion and removal at *both* ends, generalising both stack and queue. Practical uses include sliding-window max/min (monotonic deque) and browser back/forward navigation. Python's `collections.deque` is the reference implementation. In JavaScript, a doubly linked list with head and tail pointers implements a deque cleanly.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The Stack uses the array end so push/pop stay O(1) amortised — never use the front. The Queue uses a linked list so dequeue is O(1) without shifting. The balanced-parentheses check is one of the most common stack interview problems: the LIFO order naturally matches the nesting structure of brackets.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Avoid `array.shift()` as dequeue** — it is O(n) and will time-limit large inputs. Instead use a linked-list queue, or simulate with **two stacks** (enqueue onto stack 1; dequeue from stack 2 — refill stack 2 from stack 1 when empty). Each element is moved at most once, giving O(1) amortised dequeue. The two-stack queue is itself a classic interview question.

items: A stack is LIFO — push and pop happen at the same end; all operations are O(1).
A queue is FIFO — enqueue at the rear, dequeue at the front; use a linked list or circular buffer for O(1) dequeue.
Using `array.shift()` as dequeue is O(n) — a common performance trap on large inputs.
BFS uses a queue (level-order); DFS uses a stack (implicit call stack or explicit).
A deque supports O(1) insert and remove at both ends — useful for sliding-window and navigation problems.

quiz.question: Which access order does a stack enforce?
options: First-In First-Out (FIFO)
Last-In First-Out (LIFO)
Random access by index
Priority-based order
quiz.explanation: A stack is LIFO — the last item pushed is the first item popped. The JavaScript call stack works exactly this way: the most recently called function returns first.

quiz.question: Why is `array.shift()` a poor choice for `dequeue` in a high-performance queue?
options: It removes from the wrong end
It is O(n) because it shifts all remaining elements left
It returns undefined instead of the removed value
It does not work with non-integer values
quiz.explanation: `shift()` removes index 0 and shifts every subsequent element one position left — O(n). For O(1) dequeue, use a linked-list queue or circular buffer.

quiz.question: Which graph traversal algorithm uses a queue as its core data structure?
options: Depth-first search (DFS)
Dijkstra's algorithm
Breadth-first search (BFS)
Binary search
quiz.explanation: BFS explores nodes level by level. It enqueues unvisited neighbours and dequeues the next node to process. The FIFO order guarantees all nodes at distance k are visited before any at distance k+1.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of `push` and `pop` on a stack implemented with a dynamic array (using the array end)?
options: O(n) for both
O(1) for push, O(n) for pop
O(1) amortised for push, O(1) for pop
O(log n) for both
quiz.explanation: `push` (array.push) is O(1) amortised due to occasional buffer doubling. `pop` (array.pop) removes the last element with no shifting — strictly O(1).

quiz.question: The browser Back button is best modelled by which structure?
options: Queue — FIFO ordering
Stack — LIFO ordering
Min-heap — priority ordering
Hash map — O(1) lookup
quiz.explanation: Each visited page is pushed onto the history stack. Pressing Back pops the most recent page — classic LIFO. A deque models both Back and Forward together.

quiz.question: A deque (double-ended queue) supports which operations in O(1)?
options: Insert and remove at the front only
Insert and remove at the back only
Insert and remove at both front and back
Random access by index
quiz.explanation: A deque provides O(1) addFront, addRear, removeFront, and removeRear — generalising both stack and queue. Random access by index is not a deque guarantee.

quiz.question: How does the two-stack queue achieve O(1) amortised `dequeue`?
options: Always reverse stack 1 into stack 2 on every enqueue
Enqueue onto stack 1; on dequeue, if stack 2 is empty pour stack 1 into it
Use stack 1 for odd indices and stack 2 for even indices
Merge both stacks after every operation
quiz.explanation: Enqueue always pushes onto stack 1. Dequeue pops from stack 2; when stack 2 is empty, pour all of stack 1 into stack 2 (reversing order gives FIFO). Each element is moved at most once — O(1) amortised.

quiz.question: Which problem is a classic application of a stack?
options: Finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph
Checking balanced parentheses in an expression
Sorting an array in O(n log n)
Finding the kth largest element
quiz.explanation: Balanced parentheses: push open brackets onto the stack, pop on close brackets and verify the match. The stack's LIFO order naturally mirrors the nesting structure of brackets.

quiz.question: In a linked-list queue, which end is the front (dequeue) and which is the rear (enqueue)?
options: Head = rear (enqueue), tail = front (dequeue)
Head = front (dequeue), tail = rear (enqueue)
Both operations happen at the head
Both operations happen at the tail
quiz.explanation: Enqueue appends at the tail (O(1) with a tail pointer). Dequeue removes from the head (O(1) — advance head). This gives O(1) for both operations.

quiz.question: What distinguishes iterative DFS from BFS when each is implemented with an explicit data structure?
options: DFS uses a queue, BFS uses a stack
DFS explores nodes level by level; BFS explores deepest path first
DFS uses a stack giving depth-first order; BFS uses a queue giving level-order
They are identical — only the termination condition differs
quiz.explanation: DFS with an explicit stack pops the most recently pushed neighbour, diving deep before backtracking. BFS with a queue dequeues the oldest neighbour, processing all nodes at distance k before distance k+1.
